{{Short description|Stoic philosopher}}
'''Dionysius''' of [[Cyrene, Libya|Cyrene]] ({{langx|grc|Διονύσιος ὁ Κυρηναῖος}}), lived c. 150 BC, was a [[Stoicism|Stoic]] philosopher and [[mathematician]]. 

He was a pupil of [[Diogenes of Babylon]] and [[Antipater of Tarsus]].

He was famed as a mathematician, and he is probably the Dionysius whose arguments are attacked by [[Philodemus]] in his book ''On Signs'' ({{langx|la|De Signis}}),<ref>{{cite book |last=Allen |first=James |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/49863 |title=Inference from Signs: Ancient Debates about the Nature of Evidence |date=7 June 2001 |publisher=Oxford University PressOxford |isbn=978-0-19-825094-4 |page=207 |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198250944.001.0001}}</ref> where Dionysius is reported as arguing that the Sun must be very large because it reappears slowly from behind an obstruction.<ref>Barnes, J., "Pyrrhonism, Belief and Causation.  Observations on the Skepticism of Sextus Empiricus", pp. 2661–2662, in ''Aufstieg und Niedergang der römischen Welt:: Geschichte und Kultur Roms im Spiegel der neueren Forschung.'' ed. Werk, Vogt, Haase, Temporini. Walter de Gruyter. (1997).{{ISBN?}}</ref>
